summary: Chinese has no past tense: the verb is the same for yesterday, today and tomorrow (我昨天十一点睡觉 / 我每天十一点睡觉). A past event is placed in time by a time word before the verb — 昨天, 昨天晚上, 上个星期, 去年, 以前 — or simply by the situation. What Chinese marks is completion: 了 after the verb says the action is done, usually with a number or a length (我睡了八个小时 ‘I slept eight hours’); 了 at the end says a new situation holds (他起床了 ‘he’s up’); 已经 … 了 is ‘already’. A past action is denied with 没 + verb, and 了 disappears: 他没起床 ‘he didn’t get up’. Questions add 吗 or 没有: 你吃早饭了吗？ / 你吃早饭了没有？. Plain descriptions of the past — states, adjectives, 是 and 在, habits — take no 了: 昨天我很累 ‘I was tired yesterday’. 过 (S14) adds ‘ever, before’: 我去过北京. Many routine verbs are verb + object words (起床, 洗澡, 睡觉, 出门): 了 or a length go inside them, and they take no further object.

blocks.caption: Past events: a time word, then 了 for what was completed

head: Every day (habit)
Yesterday (done)
rows: 我每天七点醒。 I wake up at seven every day.
我昨天六点就醒了。 Yesterday I was awake by six.
他每天睡八个小时。 He sleeps eight hours a night.
他昨天睡了八个小时。 He slept eight hours last night.
我每天八点出门。 I leave home at eight every day.
我今天八点就出门了。 Today I was out of the door by eight.
我每天吃早饭。 I have breakfast every day.
我今天没吃早饭。 I didn’t have breakfast today.
blocks.caption: The same verb for habit and event: the frame and 了 make the difference

blocks.title: 了 is not a past tense
blocks.text: 了 marks an action as done or a situation as new — not ‘past’. No 了 for states and adjectives (昨天我很累 ‘I was tired yesterday’), for 是 and 在 (昨天我在家), for habits (以前我每天七点起床) and after 才 ‘not until’ (他十点才起床). And 了 also works in the future: 明天我吃了早饭就走 ‘tomorrow I’ll leave once I’ve had breakfast’.

blocks.title: Where 了 goes
blocks.text: With a bare object, put 了 at the end: 我吃早饭了 ‘I’ve had breakfast’. Verb + 了 + object wants more — a number (我喝了两杯咖啡), a length (我睡了八个小时) or a next step (我吃了早饭就出门了 ‘after breakfast I went out’). Both together, verb 了 … 了, means ‘so far, and still going’: 我睡了八个小时了 ‘I’ve been asleep for eight hours now’.

blocks.title: 没 swallows 了
blocks.text: 他起床了 → 他没起床 (never *他没起床了). ‘Not yet’ is 还没 … (呢): 他还没起床呢. 不 + verb is a refusal or a habit, not a past event: 他不起床 ‘he won’t get up’.

items.title: 没 — it did not happen
points: 他没吃早饭。 He didn’t have breakfast.
昨天晚上我没睡着。 I couldn’t get to sleep last night.

items.title: 不 — will not / does not (as a rule)
points: 他不吃早饭。 He doesn’t eat breakfast.
我不睡觉！ I’m not going to bed!

blocks.title: Verb–object words open up
blocks.text: Many routine verbs are verb + object (离合词): 起床, 洗澡, 睡觉, 出门, 穿衣. 了, 个, a number or a length go between the parts: 洗了个澡 ‘had a shower’, 睡了一觉 ‘had a sleep’, 出了门 ‘went out’. The whole word never takes another object, so a length goes with the bare verb: 睡了八个小时, not *睡觉了八个小时.

blocks.title: 就 and 才 with clock times
blocks.text: 就 + verb + 了: early, sooner than expected — 他六点就起床了 ‘he was up by six’. 才 + verb, without 了: late, not until — 他十点才起床 ‘he didn’t get up till ten’. The time stays before both.

blocks.title: 已经 … 了 — already
blocks.text: 已经 goes before the verb and 了 at the end: 他已经出门了 ‘he has already gone out’. With a time or an age, no verb is needed: 已经十二点了 ‘it’s already twelve’. The negative is 还没: 他还没出门 ‘he hasn’t gone out yet’.

head: Time word
Meaning
blocks.caption: Time words that place an event in the past — before the verb

blocks.title: Asking about the past
blocks.text: 你吃早饭了吗？ · 你吃早饭了没有？ ‘have you had breakfast (or not)?’ · 你昨天几点睡觉？ ‘what time did you go to bed yesterday?’ The answer echoes the verb: 吃了 / 没吃. You will also hear 你昨天几点睡的？ — 是 … 的, which asks when, where or how a past event happened, comes later with emphasis (C43).

askYourself: Is it in the past? → put a time word before the verb (昨天, 上个星期); the verb itself never changes.
Was something completed and counted (two cups, eight hours)? → verb + 了 + number + noun.
Is a new situation the point (he’s up, the holidays are over)? → 了 at the end.
Is it a state, an adjective, 是 / 在, a habit, or a sentence with 才? → no 了.
Is it negative? → 没 + verb, and drop 了 (过 stays).
Is it a verb–object word (起床, 洗澡, 睡觉)? → nothing after it; 了, 个 or a length go inside.
Is it a question? → …了吗？ or …了没有？
steps: Place the event in time: the time word comes first.
Completed → 了 (after the verb with a quantity, or at the end).
Did not happen → 没 + verb; not yet → 还没.

traps: *昨天我很累了 (for a plain past state) → 昨天我很累.
*我睡觉了八个小时 → 我睡了八个小时.
*我昨天不起床 (for ‘didn’t get up’) → 我昨天没起床.
*他十点才起床了 → 他十点才起床 (才 takes no 了).
*以前我每天七点起床了 → 以前我每天七点起床 (a habit takes no 了).
他去北京了 (has gone, is there) ≠ 他去过北京 (has been, came back).

quiz.why: 没 denies a past event and 了 goes; 他不起床了 means ‘he won’t get up any more’.
A plain past state takes no 了 — 昨天 already says when.
睡觉 already has its object; the length follows 睡 + 了.
了 follows the verb phrase and 吗 comes last.
就 … 了 = as early as; 才 means ‘not until’ and takes no 了.
洗澡 is verb + object: 了 and 个 go between the parts.
已经 stands before the verb, 了 at the end.

notes.text: Greek must choose a past form: ξύπνησα ‘I woke up (once, done)’ or ξυπνούσα ‘I used to wake up / was waking’. Chinese marks only the ‘done’ side, with 了, and only when it matters: 我醒了; the habit has no marker at all (以前我七点醒).

The Russian perfective past (проснулся, встал) is close to verb + 了 (醒了, 起床了), the imperfective past (вставал) to the bare verb with a time word. But Russian also marks gender in the past (встал / встала); the Chinese verb never changes.
Me levanté (pretérito, done) ~ 我起床了; me levantaba (imperfecto, habit) ~ 以前我…起床, without 了. Ayer ~ 昨天, before the verb.

English puts every past verb in the past tense (got up, was tired). Chinese adds 了 only for a completed event: ‘I was tired yesterday’ is 昨天我很累, with no 了, and ‘I got up at seven’ can be 我七点起床 when 昨天 already says when.
Passé composé je me suis levé ~ 我起床了; imparfait je me levais (habit) ~ no 了. Chinese has no auxiliary and no participle: the verb stays 起床.
German Perfekt (ich bin aufgestanden, ich habe geduscht) and Präteritum (ich stand auf) both put the verb into the past; Chinese has no auxiliary, no participle and no tense — 我起床了, 我洗澡了.
Hindi’s perfective (उठा ‘got up’, उठी said of a woman) marks a completed event like 了, but agrees in gender and number; Chinese 起床了 is the same for everyone.
Persian builds the past from a past stem with person endings (bidār shodam ‘I woke up’, raftam ‘I went’); Chinese verbs have no stems and no endings — 醒了, 去了.
Arabic has a past (perfect) conjugation with endings for person, number and gender (قُمْتُ ‘I got up’, قَامَتْ ‘she got up’); Chinese keeps the verb bare and adds 了 or a time word.
Hebrew conjugates the past by person (קַמְתִּי ‘I got up’, קַמְנוּ ‘we got up’); Chinese has one bare form and marks completion with 了, not tense.
Turkish -di is an obligatory past suffix (kalktım ‘I got up’); Chinese 了 marks completion and is optional — and Chinese has nothing like the reported past -miş.
Japanese -ta is a past form of the verb (起きた ‘got up’, 起きなかった ‘didn’t get up’); Chinese adds 了 to an unchanged verb, and the negative 没起床 drops it.
Korean -았/었- is an obligatory past suffix (일어났어요 ‘got up’); Chinese uses a time word, and 了 only when the event is completed.
Finnish has a past tense with person endings (heräsin ‘I woke up’, heräsit ‘you woke up’); Chinese has no tense and no endings: 我醒了, 你醒了.
Hungarian marks the past with -t / -tt and completion often with a preverb (felkeltem ‘I got up’); Chinese marks the completion with a separate 了 and has no tense or person endings.
Swahili -li- is the past (niliamka ‘I woke up’) and -me- ‘has done, and so now’ (nimeamka ‘I’m awake now’) — close to verb-了 and sentence-final 了, which in Chinese are separate words and optional.
Vietnamese works like Chinese: no tense, a time word (hôm qua ~ 昨天) and optional markers — đã for a completed or past event, rồi ~ 了 (tôi dậy rồi ~ 我起床了), chưa ~ 还没 ‘not yet’.
Inuktitut marks past time with suffixes inside the verb word (nirilauqtunga ‘I ate’); Chinese adds separate words to a verb that never changes: 我吃了.

seeAlso.note: German has two past tenses — the Perfekt with haben / sein + participle in speech (ich bin aufgestanden, ich habe geduscht) and the Präteritum in writing (ich stand auf); Chinese has no past form at all: 我起床了, with 了 only for completion.
Arabic has the perfect, a past form with endings for person, number and gender (قُمْتُ ‘I got up’); Chinese keeps the verb bare and adds 了 or a time word.
Hebrew conjugates the past by person (קַמְתִּי ‘I got up’, קַמְנוּ ‘we got up’); Chinese has one form for everyone and no tense.
了, 过 and 在 were introduced with the days (S14); here they carry the past.
